newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION - BIG IS BEAUTIFUL AND CASH IS KING - JAMES CAPEL B&K.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - BIG IS BEAUTIFUL AND CASH IS KING - JAMES CAPEL B&K.

text.p: The following is an extract from "Big is
Beautiful and Cash is King," an overview of India's top 100 companies by securities firm James Capel B&K.
The firm says heavyweights will outperform the broad market with cash-rich companies -- which can self-finance their growth -- emerging the winners.
**MARKET STRATEGY**
LIQUIDITY:
The latent demand for capital will act as a dampener to the markets. Whenever the market 'runs away', a host of cash calls will act as speed breakers.
Implementation of depository and lower long-term interest rates are two of the major indicators one has to watch for before we can witness a bull run.
Till then, we feel that supply will exceed demand, and the markets will remain sluggish - a good opportunity to pick long-term winners.

While it is almost impossible to predict the timing of a market, the liquidity factor gives a good indication. We have analysed the liquidity of the market by looking at the demand for and supply of paper flowing in the market.
DEMAND SIDE
** FII Inflows: Market returns have a strong correlation
with FII inflows - a clear evidence that they now form bulk of demand for stocks.
This year, inflows have been relatively high. Inflows will largely depend upon U.S. interest rates. We believe that these flows will continue to form the bulk of investments in the secondary market.
** Domestic Mutual Funds: With most of the sops gone, and the high interest rate scenario, mutual funds are not as attractive as they used to be.
The high rate of redemption has taken its toll. Until some major change occurs either on the policy front or in the structure of interest rates, there isn't much hope.
The fate of the two large foreign fund management firms, trying to launch domestic funds this month (Aug '96), will be a pointer to the future of domestic funds.
** Retail Investors: In the tight money supply situation and the extremely high long-term interest rate scenario, retail investors have become extinct.
In any case, retail investors as a group are always the last ones to enter, so one cannot look at them for a reversal of trend.
SUPPLY SIDE:

** Domestic primary market: Although the domestic primary market has been sluggish, it is a reflection of demand rather than supply. The latent supply is very high. Many companies that had announced public issues have postponed their plans.
** Primary GDR market: The GDR market has been fairly active this year and promises to be more so in the coming months with around $2 billion worth of fresh paper hitting the market.
THE STAGE OF THE INVESTMENT CYCLE:
The initial euphoria with which the capital markets greeted the liberalisation of the Indian economy has died down. We have entered into a phase of 'sanity'. The grind has just begun.
With a much more scarce and selective supply of capital, the 'more equal than others' will dominate. This process of 'sanity' is good for the long term as it is laying the foundation for a take-off.
The stock markets have been very volatile in the last five years. On a cursory look, the events do not seem to form any particular pattern; however, on a closer look, some pattern emerges.
With the risk of oversimplifying a complicated pattern, we are introducing a slightly different theme to define the stage of the investment cycle in India.
EUPHORIA:
* 'Hot money' chasing stocks for early gains; FIIs tasting India for the very first time.
* Sudden inflows make India the 'flavour' of the season.
* Corporates get opportunistic and announce mega expansions.
* GDRs with aggressive pricing; private placement by corporates.
* Easy money frittered away into real estate and stock markets by corporates; easy money allowed for 'other income'.
SANITY:
* 'Quality' in demand for profits and management.
* Incremental analysis for capex by investors.
* Defensive stocks 'in'.
* GDRs for quality stocks only at sensible pricing.
* Deferment/Cancellation of glamorous expansion/ diversification plans.
* Survival of the fittest - pangs of competition, liberalisation.
* Capital squeeze will lead to better allocation of resources.
* Big getting better.
CONSOLIDATION:
* Mergers and acquisitions (M&A).
* Prudent capex by industry.
* Shake-out for weaker players/industry.
* Revival of debt market.
* Revival of domestic mutual funds.
* Interest rates flattening out.
TAKE-OFF:
* Benefits of prudent capex.
* Interest rates down, equity investments up.
* Successful M&A stocks.
* Hunt for value stocks.
* Revival of small & mid caps.

The sanity phase, which began last year, will probably continue for another two years. The major problem in this stage is the scarcity of capital which will make cash-strapped companies more vulnerable.

While the consolidation phase, which is the next phase, will open up investment opportunities in the small/mid cap takeover targets, till we enter into that stage, the bigger stocks will offer as far better risk/return profile.
EARNINGS GROWTH:

Global softening of petrochemical and metal prices coupled with a decrease in import duties in the recent budget, the introduction of MAT, and a steep rise in fuel/freight costs will shrink margins and result in an earnings growth of not more than 11 percent this year.
We expect earnings to bounce back in the next year, the extent of which will depend upon global commodity prices.
What are the prospects of FY97?
This year, companies' earnings will get hit by the following factors:
** International Prices:

The depressed prices of international commodities such as petrochemicals, aluminium, steel and paper coupled with a steady decrease in import duties of these products will have an impact on the earnings growth of many of the stocks in our universe.
** Cost Increase:
A steep increase in the controlled prices of petroproducts and the subsequent increase in freight rates will result in an all-round reduction of margins.
** MAT:
The introduction of minimum alternate (MAT) tax will bring most of the companies into the tax net. The most severely hit companies are the ones which had major expansion plans coming up.
Sectors such as petrochemicals, chemicals, paper and steel, which have a 13 percent weightage in our universe, will show negative earnings growth this year.
It is only because of sectors such as automobiles, consumer goods and banks that the average earnings growth is still in double digits.
The Risks To Earnings in FY98:
While the earnings growth will slow down to 11 percent in FY97, we are forecasting a 23 percent growth in FY98.
This is because most of the factors affecting earnings in FY97 will have a one-time effect on the margins and, unless there are more changes, the earnings growth will bounce back as volumes jump.
However, one has to be cautious in reading too much in the earnings rebound. Any changes in expansion plans, due to the liquidity crunch, will tend to depress earnings.
This is a major risk to FY98 earnings. Also, the global trends of commodity prices will continue to affect overall earnings growth.
Our global house view is that most of these commodities should bounce back, which will have an overall positive impact on earnings.
VALUATIONS:
Given the earnings growth scenario, the valuations don't look as cheap as they did before, making this a stock pickers' market.

The top 100 companies are trading at 14x Mar'97 earnings, at a growth earnings multiple of 0.78x. Since we feel cash is king in the current scenario, we have used measures such as EV/EBIDT and net debt/market cap, along with PE ratios to pick the winners.
Are the valuations as cheap as they seem to be?

Although the market price/earnings multiples appear low, if we take into account the slowdown in earnings this year, a vulnerable next year and the high long-term interest rates, the valuations are not as cheap as they appear.
The Valuation of a Company Should be Higher:
* Bigger the company, relative to its sector.
* More cash-rich the company.
* Less volatile its earnings.
* If the company is less likely to tap the equity markets.
Bigger the Company, Better the Valuation:

This comes right out of our stage of the investment cycle theme. As we have emphasised at every stage, the likelihood of a bigger company not only surviving, but also emerging as a winner in this stage is much more than a smaller one, ceteris paribus.
This is based on the assumption that the bigger company will have not only better economies of scale, but also have a competitive advantage in raising resources in this environment.
More Cash-Rich the Company, Better the Valuation:
Cash is king. Again, this theme is a direct fallout of our stage in the cycle theory. In the high interest rate scenario, its importance cannot be emphasised more.
For a comparison across companies, we have used net debt as a percentage of market capitalisation as a measure of the same.
Less Volatile the Earnings, Better the Valuation:
Volatility of earnings largely depends upon the sector in which the company operates in. As one moves from a low value-additive sector to a high value-additive one, the valuations should improve.

For example, the earnings for a processor would be much more volatile than for an integrated player. This analogy can apply to services as well, for eg. while financial institutions are 'processors', they act as intermediaries to wholesale sources; banks are 'integrated' as they avail of retail sources.
Less Likely to Cash Call, Better the Valuation:
While this is definitely linked to the cash richness of a company, independently, it is a very important factor which determines the valuation.

This is based on a premise that when a company makes a cash call, the valuations are at the diktat of the investors. In simple terminology, what this means is that for a given demand, larger supply of paper will always put pressure on valuations. In the Indian context, this has largely been true for MNCs.
One of the reasons they enjoy such a premium is that they rarely make cash calls.
(The opinions expressed in this article reflect the views of the author. They should not be taken as reflecting the views of Reuters)
